submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole encodes the mathematical concept of a map/function between two objects: it peaks on the token that carries the correspondence - the arrow in f:X->Y ('\rightarrow', '\to', '\mapsto'), 'maps' plus its preposition ('to', 'onto', 'into'), 'from ... to' once a map or function has been named, 'between' after 'a map', and 'reversed' where a map is inverted - and on the words naming a map or its parts ('function', 'mapping', 'relation', 'range', 'inverse', 'one-to-one', 'image'), strongest when the map's arguments are abstract or symbolically denoted (X, Y, A, B, f, G, H, a vector, the kernel). The same strings outside a correspondence leave it near zero ('he climbed onto the roof', 'the train goes from X to Y', 'the bomb annihilates the city', 'a link between the two spaces', 'encryption converts the message into ciphertext'), as does mathematical prose that states no correspondence ('the polynomial has three real roots', 'the sequence converges uniformly').

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
During the third quarter the plant shipped more than forty thousand units, a figure that the operations team attributes to the new scheduling software and to the decision to run two shifts instead of three. The function of the quality assurance group is to sample every batch before it leaves the floor, and to flag any deviation from the specification sheet. That group reports directly to the plant manager, who reviews the weekly numbers with the regional director each Friday morning.

The warehouse receives pallets from the supplier in the north yard and loads them onto trucks bound for the retail stores along the coast. Most orders arrive before ten in the morning, which leaves the afternoon free for restocking and for the cycle counts that the auditors require. Last year the team converted the old paper logs into a digital system, and the error rate fell by roughly half within two months.

A wide range of products passes through this facility, from small replacement parts to complete assemblies, and each line has its own tolerances and its own inspection routine. The larger assemblies are awkward to handle, so they are moved on custom cradles rather than on standard pallets. Supervisors rotate through the lines every few weeks, partly to spread expertise and partly because the repetitive work is easier to sustain when the tasks change.

Management has been discussing a second facility for some time. The argument in favor is straightforward: demand in the coastal region keeps growing, and shipping from this site adds two days and a meaningful freight cost to every order. The argument against is that a second site doubles the overhead in supervision, maintenance and compliance, and the company has only just finished paying down the debt from the last expansion. A consultant's report, circulated in June, recommended waiting at least a year before committing.

Staffing remains the difficult question. Skilled machinists are scarce in the region, and the training program takes nearly eighteen months before a new hire can work unsupervised on the more demanding parts. The plant has had some success with apprenticeships arranged through the local technical college, but the intake is small and the dropout rate is high. Wages have risen faster here than in comparable plants elsewhere, which the finance team watches closely.

For the moment the plan is to squeeze more capacity out of the existing building. Two of the older lines will be reorganized over the winter shutdown, and the loading dock will be extended so that more trucks can be handled at once. If the numbers hold through the spring, the board will revisit the question of a second site, but nobody expects a decision before the next fiscal year.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
In the previous lecture we reviewed vector spaces over an arbitrary field and fixed notation for bases and coordinates. Today we continue with linear transformations, and we stay in finite dimension so that every statement can be checked against a matrix.

Recall that a basis of a space $V$ is a linearly independent spanning set, and that every vector has a unique expression as a finite linear combination of basis elements. The coefficients in that expression are the coordinates of the vector, and they depend on the basis chosen. If we change the basis, the coordinates change by an invertible matrix, which we called the change of basis matrix. Two matrices related in this way represent the same underlying transformation, and that is why we are free to choose coordinates adapted to a particular problem.

We then spent some time on subspaces. The kernel and the image of a linear transformation turned out to be subspaces, of the domain and of the codomain respectively, and their dimensions are linked by the rank-nullity theorem. That theorem is the first genuine structural result of the course, and it will reappear several times below. In particular, injectivity is equivalent to the kernel being trivial, and surjectivity is equivalent to the image being the whole codomain.

The exercises for this week ask you to compute kernels and images for a number of small matrices, and to decide in each case whether the transformation is injective or surjective. Several of you asked whether the two questions are related; the rank-nullity theorem answers that they are, but only once the dimensions are known. Please write out the argument rather than quoting the theorem, since the point of the exercise is to see where the dimension count comes from.

Today we want to go further and treat the transformation itself, rather than any matrix that represents it, as the primary object. The reason is that several constructions become cleaner once coordinates are removed. Composition of transformations is just composition of functions, and the inverse of an invertible transformation is again linear. Moreover the collection of all linear transformations between two fixed spaces is itself a vector space, with addition and scalar multiplication defined pointwise, and this observation will let us speak about dual spaces without any additional machinery.

We can now state the central definition of the section. A linear map $T: V \to W$ is called an isomorphism when there exists a linear map $S: W \to V$ such that the composite $ST$ is the identity on $V$ and the composite $TS$ is the identity on $W$. When such an $S$ exists it is unique, and we write $S = T^{-1}$. Two spaces that admit an isomorphism between them are said to be isomorphic, and from the point of view of linear algebra they are indistinguishable: they have the same dimension, the same number of basis elements, and the same lattice of subspaces.

Two warnings before we finish. First, an isomorphism is not the same thing as a bijection of the underlying sets; the linear structure has to be respected, and there are plenty of bijections that are not linear. Second, the definition above is deliberately coordinate-free, and you should resist the temptation to prove statements about isomorphisms by choosing a basis unless the coordinate argument genuinely simplifies matters. Next week we will use these ideas to define the dual of a linear transformation and to show that the double dual of a finite-dimensional space is naturally isomorphic to the space itself.
